answers.explanation: Longest match means most specific. The /24 is an exception carved out of a bigger block.
20 = 00010100. Its first five bits, 00010, match 200.23.16.0/21. It doesn't match either 24 route.
It matches the /24 and the /21 for 200.23.24.0. The /24 is longer, so interface 1.
31 = 00011111: the first five bits 00011 match 200.23.24.0/21, but 31 isn't 24, so the /24 doesn't match.
It matches everything, but at length 0 it's the shortest possible prefix, so it only wins when nothing else matches.
The don't-care bits are the host part after the prefix, the asterisks in the binary table.
Every entry is compared in parallel, so the size of the table doesn't change the lookup time.
It's expensive and power-hungry. That's part of why route aggregation and small tables matter.
An ISP can advertise one big block while a more specific route points part of it somewhere else.
